absent: Locking discipline for the global IRQ source table and ISA to GSI map under concurrent registration and lookup.
Numeric values of legacy limits, maximum IRQ sources, maximum IOAPICs and invalid IRQ sentinel.
Full layouts of interrupt source, IOAPIC descriptor, GSI interval and domain configuration records beyond observed fields.
Boot sequencing that invokes MADT parsers and transitions from early to hotplug registration.
Behaviour of core GSI registration, ELCR level marking, SCI penalisation and IRQ domain operations.
Initialisation and lifetime of global counts, GSI top, dynamic IRQ base and disable flags.
Suspend and resume use of saved register buffers.

findings.text: The lane exposes a small IOAPIC registry. One routine registers a new unit from identifier, physical address, base global interrupt and domain configuration. Two routines translate a global interrupt to the owning unit index and to the pin offset inside that unit. Three accessors reveal the stored identifier, version and address for a unit index, plus a helper returning the interval object and a helper computing pin count from interval bounds. A macro iterates unit indexes from start up to the current count.

Interrupt source description is built and stored through four paths. One routine appends a source descriptor to a global table after suppressing exact duplicates. Another converts a global interrupt to unit and pin and records an ISA bus entry carrying caller polarity and trigger. A legacy override wrapper validates the legacy number, normalises a known faulty timer trigger, delegates to the converter and updates the ISA to global map while clearing a conflicting identity entry. A PCI path ignores non PCI devices or absent IOAPIC support and otherwise records a PCI bus entry derived from bus number, device function and pin.

Global to Linux IRQ translation is layered. One function maps a legacy ISA number through a table, failing when out of range or marked invalid. Another maps any global interrupt to an IRQ, passing through directly in PIC mode and otherwise resolving override polarity and trigger before registration. Registration itself forwards to a core helper, with a PIC variant that marks level interrupts in the edge level control. Override lookup finds the owning unit and pin, locates the stored descriptor for the interrupt type and decodes level versus edge and low versus high from flag bits with bus dependent defaults and an EISA control check in one build and direct pass through in the other.

ACPI table parsing provides three entry points plus two system control helpers. The IOAPIC parser validates the subtable, selects legacy versus dynamic domain kind from the global base and registers the unit. The interrupt override parser validates, records that a legacy source was overridden, diverts the system control interrupt to special setup, applies timer skip and pin polarity fixes for source zero, and otherwise applies a legacy override. The NMI source parser only validates and logs, implementing no storage. Control setup supplies default level and low values, honours command line flag overrides, chooses override versus direct registration by legacy range, penalises the interrupt and stashes the chosen global. A PIC helper programs the trigger bit in the edge level control ports.

Each IOAPIC owns a closed global interval with base and end. Lookup scans all units in index order and returns the first whose interval contains the queried value, reporting failure when no unit exists or none matches. Pin number is the offset of the global from the interval base and is only valid when the unit index is non negative and the global does not exceed the interval end. Pin count equals end minus base plus one. Registration rejects a new interval that overlaps any existing interval endpoint.

Legacy ISA numbers map to globals through a table initially identity. An override for a legacy number below the legacy limit clears the identity entry at the target global when that entry still maps to itself, preventing duplicate globals, then stores the new mapping. Timer source zero with level trigger is coerced to edge to avoid a storm. The control path defaults unspecified trigger to level and unspecified polarity to low before applying command line overrides. A flag array records which legacy sources received overrides, and a global remembers the control override.

IOAPIC identifiers are unique system wide. One build delegates legacy Intel machines without extended APIC support to a routine that tracks used identifiers in a static bitmap seeded from the physical CPU map, rejects the broadcast value by falling back to the hardware register, scans for the first free value below broadcast, records the choice, programs the hardware when different and verifies the write. Modern handling in the same routine returns the requested value unchanged. An alternate build tracks identifiers used by already registered IOAPICs, prefers the requested value, then the current hardware value, then the first free value in a larger space, programming and verifying the hardware choice.

A single raw spinlock with interrupt state saving guards IOAPIC register access for version and redirection size reads and for identifier assignment sequences that read, optionally write and re read the identifier register. The lock is held across each read modify verify group so concurrent registration or probing cannot interleave index and data operations or allocate the same identifier.

State centres on a fixed size array of IOAPIC descriptors indexed by registration order. Each entry holds a configuration block with type, usability flags, physical address, identifier and version, a global interval with base and end, an IRQ domain pointer plus its configuration copy, a register count that doubles as present marker, and an optional saved register buffer sized by register count. Interrupt sources are fixed records carrying kind, interrupt type, combined polarity and trigger flags, source bus and source IRQ, and destination APIC plus destination pin. Domain configuration carries a kind tag, operations pointer and optional device link.

Observed ABI facts state that source descriptors use an interrupt source type with plain interrupt kind and combined flags packing trigger above polarity. ACPI edge maps to one encoding and level to another, with active high versus low distinguished. Polarity and trigger each have default, high or edge, reserved and low or level values, with bus dependent defaults resolving PCI toward low and level and ISA toward high and edge. Broadcast identifier is fifteen. Register zero carries identifier, register one carries version and entry count where stored count is maximum index so usable entries add one, register two participates in all ones detection. Access uses separate index and data ports reached through a per unit fixed mapping plus page offset. Edge level control uses two ports with one bit per legacy line.

Registration proceeds through ordered states. It rejects zero address and duplicate address, claims the first entry whose register count is zero, initialises type and usability, installs a fixed mapping with memory encryption protection honoured, and aborts with mapping teardown when all probed registers read all ones. It then assigns identifier and fetches version and entry count, computes the GSI end, rejects overlap with any existing interval, stores the interval, copies domain configuration with empty domain, and for hotplug time calls creates the IRQ hierarchy and allocates the suspend buffer. Finally it advances the global GSI top, unit count and present marker and logs the resulting span. Early boot calls defer domain creation and buffer allocation.

Failure handling is explicit. Appending beyond the maximum source count halts, as does exhausting APIC identifiers below broadcast. A hardware identifier write that does not read back fails in one build and traps in the other. Out of range GSI to unit or pin translation warns and fails rather than indexing outside the table. Zero or duplicate physical address, full unit table, all ones registers and overlapping GSI intervals each abort registration with teardown of the fixed mapping. Invalid polarity or trigger encodings warn and fall back to low and level. Out of range legacy override and ignored timer override only warn.

Override queries resolve through stored descriptors. Lookup is disabled entirely when a global disable flag is set. Otherwise the GSI maps to unit and pin, and a linear search finds the first descriptor matching the interrupt type, target pin and either exact destination identifier or broadcast all. Polarity and trigger are then decoded from flag subfields with defaults consulting a per bus PCI marker and, for trigger defaults on EISA capable builds, the edge level control bit for the source IRQ. Missing unit, pin or descriptor yields failure with outputs left at edge and high.

IRQ domain creation is skipped for invalid kind. Otherwise a firmware node is taken from the device when present or allocated as a named node keyed by APIC identifier, a single cell spec carrying the identifier locates a generic MSI parent, and a hierarchical domain is created with size equal to pin count and the unit index as argument. Failure frees an allocated node and reports resource errors. Legacy and strict kinds advance the dynamic IRQ base past the interval end.
